claim: Debugging is the single biggest stumbling block for non-technical workshop participants and instructors compensate by teaching attendees to query the AI to explain errors rather than fix code themselves.
quote: The most significant challenge participants faced was debugging—a common hurdle for those without technical backgrounds. The workshop addressed this by teaching attendees to interact with AI systems to grasp fundamental coding concepts and resolve errors systematically.

claim: Workshop instructors recommend telling participants to abandon broken apps and rebuild rather than try to patch them after the session.
quote: Instructor Agrim Singh advised that 'it is often more efficient to abandon a flawed concept rather than trying to fix it,' reframing failure as useful feedback for rapid pivoting.

claim: Across 170 Lovable-built apps shipped by beginners, authorization was inverted so unauthenticated visitors had full data access while logged-in users were blocked — the kind of breakage participants will hit days after going home.
quote: Authenticated users were blocked. Unauthenticated visitors had full access to all data across 170 production applications.

claim: The root cause of post-deployment breakage in vibe-coded apps is the absence of any automated testing layer between AI generation and the live URL, leaving non-technical builders no way to catch regressions.
quote: The root cause across all cases: no automated testing layer between AI generation and production deployment.

claim: Lovable's primary continuity pattern is a 160K-member Discord plus recurring topical office hours (e.g. Security Office Hours) and a community@lovable.dev email, which is the template most vibe-coding platforms now offer alumni.
quote: 160K+ Discord members ... Security Office Hours (May 28, 2026, Online) ... community@lovable.dev

claim: Facilitators at the Berkeley ALS vibe-coding sessions concluded that one workshop is never enough and committed to a series of follow-up workshops, because participants cannot keep pace with tooling change alone.
quote: It's unreal. It's pretty much impossible to keep up ... The Photon Science Computing group has scheduled an entire series of additional workshops.

claim: ALS facilitators printed take-home reminders such as the 'Rule of Two' (if you repeat an instruction more than twice, put it in a file, not a prompt) and explicit warnings about API-key leakage.
quote: Wiebke Koepp introduced the Rule of Two—if instructions repeat more than twice, they belong in a file rather than prompts ... David Abramov warned about protecting API keys

claim: The two failure modes that matter most for non-technical alumni are exposed databases (plaintext passwords, hard-coded API keys) and 'works on my machine = shipped' assumptions that collapse the moment a second user opens the URL.
quote: Never Opening the Actual Database — Security holes like plaintext passwords and hardcoded API keys remain invisible until production ... 'Works on My Machine' = Shipped — Performance issues and missing safeguards only surface under real user traffic and data volume.

claim: Recommended take-home practice for laymen is a project-level CLAUDE.md (or equivalent rules file) so future AI sessions don't drift from the conventions the workshop set up.
quote: No CLAUDE.md — Without documented project constraints, each new session drifts further from established conventions and patterns.

claim: A 2026 hackathon retrospective documents the canonical post-event failure: prototypes that 'looked done but weren't', collapsing the moment real users tried them — the warning facilitators should bake into the take-home card.
quote: Features that looked done but weren't. Prototypes with beautiful UI and filler copy where the actual thinking should have been ... things got uncomfortable ... didn't hold up.

claim: Anthropic's Teach For All program codifies the now-standard post-workshop stack for non-technical learners: monthly office hours plus a persistent Claude Connect community across 60+ countries for daily peer Q&A.
quote: monthly office hours with the Anthropic team ... Claude Connect serves as the community's ongoing learning hub with more than 1,000 educators representing 60+ countries exchanging prompts, use cases, and discoveries through daily peer-to-peer conversation.

claim: The Vibe Coders Collective shows that an in-person workshop's afterlife typically runs on Meetup + a separate hub site (vibecoders.global) + LinkedIn rather than a single Discord, so cheat-sheets should list multiple re-entry points.
quote: https://vibecoders.global ... Find us also at [LinkedIn] ... 28 past events publicly
